The country that lost hot beer

Mayhew counted the men who sold hot beer off boats in the Pool of London. Britain still has recipes for it. What is harder to find is anything like the trade he describes.

Before dawn, in the Pool of London, a man rowed out to the ships with a fire burning in the bottom of his boat.

He was selling hot beer. In 1851 Henry Mayhew counted men like him and wrote the chapter up as a trade rather than a curiosity, Of the River Beer-Sellers, or Purl-Men: what a boat cost, what a licence cost, who bought. They worked in short, broad skiffs, rang a heavy bell as they came, and were hailed by the coal-whippers and lightermen with a shout of “Purl ahoy”. They were licensed from Waterman’s Hall, like the watermen themselves.

In winter fog, when the watermen lost their bearings and shouting got them nowhere, they steered home by the purl-man’s bell. Boak & Bailey went through the same chapter in 2018 and followed the boats further than we are going to here.

What was in the cans had already changed by the time Mayhew got there. Purl had been ale with wormwood in it, bitter and medicinal, although Mayhew could not say why that was called purl: he notes only that the philologist Nathan Bailey used the word that way. By 1851, Mayhew writes, “the wormwood is unknown; and what is sold under the name of purl is beer warmed nearly to boiling heat, and flavoured with gin, sugar, and ginger”.

The receipt for common purl that John Bickerdyke printed in 1889 runs to Roman wormwood, gentian root, sweet sedge, snake root, horseradish, dried orange peel, juniper berries and the kernels of Seville oranges, all left standing in beer for some months, and the writer he had it from thought a pound or two of galingale would improve it.

Purl was not the only ale with a herb cupboard in it. William Butler, physician at the court of James I, gave his name to a purging ale made, by the account Ivan Day traces, by hanging a canvas bag of senna, polypody of oak, agrimony, maidenhair and scurvy grass in a barrel of strong ale, and sold, the story goes, only by taverns licensed to hang his head on the sign. Gregg Smith counts it among the hot spiced beers of the early 1600s. One of those taverns is still open: the Old Doctor Butler’s Head in Mason’s Avenue, off Moorgate, on a site that has had a pub on it since 1610.

The Early Purl House

Robert Patten, scholar in residence at the Dickens House Museum, divides that London up by what it drank: beer, ale and gin for the labouring classes, wine and sherry for the rich, and punches for the middle, “because they had boiling water”.

Indoors it had its own equipment and its own premises. Dickens gave the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters, in Our Mutual Friend, “comfortable fireside tin utensils, like models of sugar loaf hats”, pointed so that they could be driven into the glowing part of the fire “when they mulled your ale, or heated for you those delectable drinks, Purls, Flip, and Dog’s Nose”. The pub advertised itself on its own door-posts as “The Early Purl House”. W. T. Marchant quotes the passage in In Praise of Ale of 1888, in a chapter he simply calls Warm Ale.

The Beer Connoisseur notes that instruments for mulling ale in a coal fire, looking a little like slippers made of copper, still turn up in country antique shops.

Marchant has buttered ale, which a seventeenth century French visitor describes as cinnamon, sugar, butter and beer brewed without hops, and which Pepys drinks in March 1669 before taking a coach. There is egg flip and egg hot and posset and dog’s nose. There is lamb’s wool, the spiced ale with roasted crab apples burst into it, which we have written about before. Marchant gives the reason for all of it in one line: when beer was the staple drink morning, noon and night, people naturally wanted their breakfast beer warm.

What Dickens drank

The Six Jolly Fellowship Porters in Our Mutual Friend sold purl, dog’s nose and port negus, and in The Holly Tree the narrator reaches the Peacock on a night of ice in the Thames to find “everybody drinking hot purl, in self-preservation”, takes a little himself, and finds it uncommonly good. The Old Curiosity Shop has the equipment: Codlin calls for a pint of warm ale at the Jolly Sandboys, the iron goes “far down in the fire” to get at the bright places, and what comes back has “that creamy froth upon the surface which is one of the happy circumstances attendant on mulled malt”.

Most of the rest is not beer. Robert Patten counts up the others: the Smoking Bishop of red wine and ruby port that Scrooge pours Bob Cratchit at the end of A Christmas Carol, sherry punch, negus, and a wassail of dry sherry, cider and brandy. Adam Selzer has been making them one at a time, egg-hot and sherry flip and Athol Brose among them.

One more belongs here. In Three Detective Anecdotes of 1850 a policeman offers a witness a drain of half-and-half, which Boak & Bailey take back to an 1820 treatise on adulteration: every publican had mild and old sent to him by the brewer, and a drinker who mixed the two himself was shaving the price of his pint.

Decline

Warm beer was once prescribed as the healthier choice. Digestion was understood as cooking: it was taken as a given, the food historian Rachel Laudan told the Atlantic, that digesting was “cooking in the fires of the stomach”, and nothing damped those fires like a cold wet drink. The 1641 treatise that Marchant reprints whole, Warm Beer; or, a Treatise wherein is declared by Many Reasons, that Beer so qualified is far more wholesome than that which is drunk cold, makes the case through dead princes: the Dauphin, son of Francis I, “a lusty strong gentleman” who was hot at tennis, drank cold, fell sick and died. The ode printed in front of it finishes, “that man unwise that drinks his liquor cold”.

The name moved. The Gin Is In traces purl through the cocktail books and finds that by William Terrington’s manual of 1869, often called the first British cocktail book, a purl is warmed beer with eggs beaten into it and a glass of spirit that need not be gin. Which is to say it had become a flip.

Cold beer also became easier to serve year-round. Michael Carver, who interprets colonial brewing for a living, puts it plainly: before refrigeration beer was served at cellar temperature, and “as the 19th century progressed, mulled beers faded from view. With the introduction of lager beer and artificial refrigeration, cold beer could be made available year-round.”

Elsewhere

Refrigeration reached everywhere, and in some places the warm drink stayed anyway.

Boak & Bailey, driven into a pub by a London fog in 2007 and finding the beer off, switched to mulled wine and remembered drinking hot spiced beer with honey and ginger in the south of Poland, then asked why Britain had no equivalent. In Poland grzane piwo is ordinary: on the Christmas market stalls in December as a matter of course, and in the Stary Rynek at the end of a cold day’s flat hunting, which is how one American first met it. In Bohemia there is a recipe for teplé pivo in Karolina Vávrová’s Prague cookbook of 1873, and an emperor drinking Glühbier cooked with ginger and cinnamon in a novel of 1871, both of which Beer Culture turned up. In Hungary small breweries are taking it up now, and a brewery manager quoted by Hello Hungary gives the rule, which is never to boil it: 60 to 65 degrees and no more.

Germany had the belief as well. Beer Syndicate takes it to Johann Krünitz’s Oeconomische Encyclopädie, where Warmbier is what grandparents drank in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries as the healthy alternative to coffee, and where it is not warmed beer so much as beer heated and then built up with eggs, flour, butter, ginger, nutmeg, salt and sugar. The Christmas markets still sell the drink: Boak & Bailey found a Glühbier stand at Dresden in 2008, although the Glühbier was Liefmans, which is Belgian, and the Germans around them looked bemused.

Germany and Austria also kept a separate technique. Bierstacheln puts a hot iron into a malty beer so the residual sugars caramelise on it. Hop Culture has it crossing the Atlantic. Eric Larkin, who brews Czech lagers at Cohesion in Denver and pokes beer at pop-ups there with two other breweries, told Beer Connoisseur that the iron does less to the temperature than a percolator and more to the head. It gives the carbonation somewhere to come out, so the glass fills with a pillowy, faintly caramel foam, and drinkers kept coming back to ask him to poke it again.

And to Texas. Strange Land Brewery in Austin hold an annual poking event, and told Food & Wine that “rather than duplicate the original, we adapted the tradition to our own context”. The original runs in spring when the bock arrives. Theirs is in autumn, and instead of a bock they poke an imperial bourbon pumpkin porter.

Portland has the other kind. Threshold Brewing serve grzaniec because the owner is Polish and wanted his own winter on the bar; Jeff Alworth found them doing it and noted that they build it on a five per cent grisette, and that in Poland an ordinary lager is the usual base.

Purl comes back

Britain still has the recipes. BBC Good Food will tell you to warm a golden ale with apple juice, brandy and spices and not let it boil. What it no longer has is anyone rowing it out to the ships. The name did come back to London for a while: a basement bar in Marylebone opened as Purl in 2010, named for the drink and serving its own version of it. The same address trades as Dive now.

Hyde Park Winter Wonderland, where the rollercoaster is the Wiesn’s own travelling steel, has an official mulled cider partner. Brothers say they are pouring warm Spiced Toffee Apple and Mulled Apple and Rum across its bars again this winter. The beer is a Helles called Bavarian Gold in a 568ml stein.

The name keeps resurfacing in North America. Sonoma Springs of Sonoma, California, brewed a Green Purl, which the Guardian noticed in 2010. The brewery’s own tasting card calls it a gruit of about 6.8 per cent, aged in a French Cabernet barrel, wormwood the main ingredient and six more herbs and roots behind it: orange peel, juniper berries, galangal root, gentian root, calamus root and horseradish. Set that against Bickerdyke. The calamus is his sweet sedge, and the gentian, horseradish, orange peel and juniper are all his as well. The galangal is the galingale Bickerdyke’s source suggested adding. Untappd says it is no longer brewed.

Howl Brewing’s Merry Windsor Purl Ale is six per cent, from a nano-brewery on Mills Road in North Saanich, British Columbia. Howl’s brewer, Dan Van Netten, told the Eagle Valley News in 2021 that he builds his from wormwood, horseradish and black pepper, that he takes the name from The Merry Wives of Windsor, and that purl was the most unpopular beer he ever made, although he liked it himself.

Rushford & Sons Brewhouse of Upton, Massachusetts, make a third, 3.1 per cent, listed as an English pale mild and described by the brewery as “an historic style dating back as far as Shakespearean times, bittered with wormwood and orange peel rather than modern hops”.

Rushford’s purl has one review on BeerAdvocate. The reviewer drank it on draught in April and wrote down fresh whole grain bread, toasted biscuit, caramel, toffee nuts, and then “mild bitter earthy hop, drier finish”. He finished: “different than I’m used to for an English mild, but decent beer regardless.”

Whatever he tasted, by the brewery’s account it was not a modern hop.

A hundred and seventy-five years earlier, Mayhew stood on the Thames among men who sold purl every morning of their lives and found that not one of them knew what the word meant.

PINtPOINT shows where drinkers have recently logged a beer, and how long ago.
